topComments.author: d-us-vb
topComments.text: This is rather interesting. But it misses the point somewhat. The problem is whether or not we want to view code as a medium of communication between other humans vs code as an abstract machine that solves a problem. We know that "programs" in the general sense are fairly objective entities that can be studied objectively, which is where the famous Sussman line about this comes from. But as a language for expressing execution semantics that a machine can then execute to produce a desirable effect on the real world (a solution to a problem), we would not expect such code to be written with other humans in mind, and as lisp is a strictly more expressive language (both for expressing the meaning of an algorithm that other humans will be able to study and understand and that a machine can execute), and that more people who program are concerned with producing a solution to a problem, the "curse of lisp" is the logical conclusion. But it's overblown. There exist many excellent and fairly complete libraries for Lisp: Closer MOP, UIOP, ASDF, Bordeaux Threads, etc. And no surprise, these libraries are virtually ubiquitous and considered (at least by me) to be more or less extensions to the language. And these libraries are written in a fairly readable style that anyone can go and try to understand the code. Secondly, the curse isn't really much of a curse at all. It is more likely to yield more robust programs. The assumption that code reuse through libraries increases software quality doesn't really hold up in practice: libraries that are "complete" tend to add bloat to applications; managing different versions of libraries on the same platform leads to arguments about static vs. dynamic linking, and so on and so forth. Ever had to debug .so versioning bugs on Linux? It's not fun. And yet, that is par for the course if you try to persist in the notion that "libraries and code reuse is always better than reinventing the wheel". As a reaction to the utter failures that have occurred due to following that ideology, entire programming communities have popped up to fight it, particularly the "Handmade Hero" that became Better Software Conferences as well as "Software Should Work". And while those people aren't a huge fan of Lisp, they really do embody the Lisp mindset of "don't be afraid of building your own system in your own solution's language". And this does usually yield nicer systems to work with because programming is theory building: bringing in different ready-made libraries introduces conflicting theories that requires even more glue code to rectify and the glue code rarely foresees all the discrepancies. And so bugs appear in the integrations between them. That's not to say that increasing "the curse of lisp" always yields higher quality. The kinds of developers that make great software with that mindset are the ones that are allergic to inconsistency at any level and so squash bugs as quickly as possible and that is what leads their software to be better. But on the practical side of programming work, you feel a lot less inhibited in trying to fix bugs when you're certain you understand the code and how the implementor decided to map the problem domain onto the range of possible solutions. This is where the issue with LLMs comes in: if programming is theory building (which I firmly believe), then what we're really after with using LLMs to generate code is a more effective technique of translating high level theory of the problem into the low level code that executes to solve the problem. As such, maybe vibe coding can work if the vibe coder diligently keeps in their mind what they're after. But usually what that means is writing notes about the desirable properties of the resultant application. And then they're just back to theory building... just at a somewhat higher level.

topComments.author: Veserv
topComments.text: Yes, basically all buffering should use work-or-time based flushing. Work-based flushing exists to batch work to amortize overhead. It allows you to tune how much time you spend in overhead in a work period. However, this can result in unbounded delay. Time-based flushing targets a worst-case latency in low throughput environments. This ensures you do not get unbounded delays. Interestingly, this also allows you to tune how much time you spend in overhead in a work period. So, with work-or-time based flushing what you are really tuning is how much time you are willing to spend in overhead in a work period and balancing that against latency. As a nit, the article calls this a derivative of Nagle’s algorithm, but it is basically the opposite. Nagle’s algorithm is about batching until acknowledgement with no mention of time. In fact, the lack of time-based flushing in Nagle’s algorithm is why it interacts so poorly with TCP Delayed Ack.

stackOverflowQuestions.title: How does PolarDB for MySQL implement automatic partition creation, and why doesn't native MySQL support this feature?
stackOverflowQuestions.bodyExcerpt: I am investigating a specific DDL/DML behavior difference between Alibaba Cloud PolarDB for MySQL (8.0 compatible) and native MySQL Community Edition 8.0 regarding Range Partitioning. Specifically, I am looking at the ability to automatically create new partitions when inserted data exceeds the maximum defined range, without needing a LESS THAN (MAXVALUE) catch-all partition or manual ALTER TABLE intervention. The Context & Native MySQL Limitation: In native MySQL 8.0, if I create a table partitioned by month: -- Native MySQL 8.0 CREATE TABLE orders ( order_id BIGINT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT, order_date DATETIME NOT NULL, amount DECIMAL(10,2), PRIMARY KEY (order_id, order_date) ) ENGINE=InnoDB PARTITION BY RANGE (YEAR(order_date) * 100 + MONTH(order_date)) ( PARTITION p202310 VALUES LESS THAN (202311), PARTITION p202311 VALUES LESS THAN (202312), PARTITION p202312 VALUES LESS THAN (202401) ); If I attempt to insert a row with order_date = '2024-01-15', native MySQL throws an error: ERROR 1526 (HY000): Table has no partition for value 202401 To prevent this in native MySQL, DBAs usually have to do one of two things: Define a catch-all partition: PARTITION pmax VALUES LESS THAN (MAXVALUE). However, this makes future partition management (like dropping old partitions or splitting the max partition) cumbersome. Implement external automation (e.g., cron jobs, Event Scheduler, or application-level logic) to periodically run ALTER TABLE ... ADD PARTITION before the boundary is reached. The Discrepancy in PolarDB for MySQL: PolarDB for MySQL supports an automatic partition creation feature natively. By using the INTERVAL syntax (or enabling automatic partition extension), the database engine automatically generates a new physical partition when an INSERT hits a value beyond the current highest boundary. -- PolarDB for MySQL CREATE TABLE orders ( order_id BIGINT NOT NULL AUTO_INCREMENT, order_date DATETIME NOT NULL, amount DECIMAL(10,2), PRIMARY KEY (order_id, order_date) ) E
